newsitem.title: USA: Testimonials offered for accused British nanny.
newsitem.headline: Testimonials offered for accused British nanny.

text.p: Lawyers for a 19-year-old British nanny, accused of killing a 9-month-old boy left in her charge, have submitted letters from her family and her vicar in an effort to persuade a judge to grant bail.

Louise Woodward, who spent her 19th birthday in a Massachusetts prison, "comes from a family of good moral character and reputation," wrote the Rev. John Hudghton, who was serving with the Royal Air Force but was the Church of England parish vicar for Woodward's family in Chester.

"In my opinion and professional judgment she strongly reflects her good upbringing in her own character," he added. He said he "knew her as a good natured, trustworthy, honest, intelligent, capable, balanced and perhaps most importantly a kind young lady."
Woodward, who has surrendered her passport, has been jailed since early February charged with the murder of Matthew Eappen.

The infant was shaken for at least 60 seconds, his brain bouncing against his skull before his head was slammed against a hard surface with a force, prosecutors said, that was equal to being thrown to the sidewalk from a a second-floor window.
Prosecutors opposed any bail for Woodward arguing she would present a risk of flight.
But Woodward's lawyers, Andrew Good and Harvey Silverglate, hoped to convince Suffolk Superior Court Judge Hiller Zobel otherwise at a hearing on Monday.

They suggested in letters submitted on Tuesday she be placed under house arrest at the home of a local lawyer with ties to the British consulate and be monitored by an electronic bracelet. In addition, Woodward's mother offered the family home, valued at $228,200 (140,000 sterling), as security.

Finally to support their claims that a British national should be granted bail, Woodward's lawyers submitted an affadavit from Manhattan lawyer Michael Dowd, who represented Caroline Beale, a British woman who tried to smuggle her dead baby on a flight from New York to England.
She eventually was granted bail by a New York court. The conditions for bail included passport surrender, the pledge of Beale's family home and being kept under house arrest at a neighbour.

Beale pleaded guilty to second degree manslaughter and was sentenced in March last year to eight months in prison, which she had already served while awaiting trial, five years probation and one year of psychiatric treatment. She was originally charged with second degree murder.
